item.description:
# Reverse-a-function drill — 2026-10-31
Target: Windows x86-64 (args in `ecx`, `edx`).
Reverse this short function to equivalent C:
```asm mystery: mov eax, ecx mov ecx, edx shr eax, cl and eax, 1 ret ```
Why does the function copy `edx` into `ecx` before shifting?
Answer:
```c unsigned mystery(unsigned x, unsigned n) { return (x >> n) & 1; // value of bit n of x } ```
- On x86 a variable shift count must live in `cl`; `shr eax, edx` doesn't exist, so the 2nd arg (`edx`) is moved into `ecx` after `x` has been saved to `eax`. - `shr` is logical (zero-fill), so bit `n` lands in bit 0; `and eax,1` masks off everything above it. - The count is masked to 5 bits by the CPU for 32-bit operands, so `n >= 32` behaves like `n & 31`.
